profiles.meeting_scenario: A hospital legal planning meeting to prepare the trust’s response strategy to a threatened negligence and informed-consent claim arising from a patient’s cancer treatment pathway, where the claimant’s solicitors cite the article 'Evidence based medicine: a movement in crisis?' to argue that the clinicians followed rigid guideline-driven care without adequately individualising treatment. The meeting takes place three days before a pre-action response drafting session. The agenda is to decide what factual materials to gather, which internal and external legal workstreams need to be started, who will handle witness preparation, and what timeline will govern the first internal case plan. The expected outcome is a shared plan for collecting the clinical record, commissioning an initial expert view, identifying the clinicians to contact, and producing a 'chronology and issues list' for counsel.

members.name: Amira Shah
members.expertise: Defending hospital trusts in consent, negligence, and documentation disputes; coordinating external counsel and medical experts
members.background: Amira trained at a national healthcare litigation firm and now leads early case assessment for complex hospital claims, especially those involving treatment-pathway decisions and contested guideline use.
members.private_state: Amira wants a tightly scoped, litigation-ready first package that can be sent to chambers quickly without creating unnecessary internal noise, and she is concerned about preserving legal privilege while avoiding commitments before she sees the full oncology record.
hidden_assumptions: A 'chronology' for this stage means a lawyer-built, privileged chronology focused on legally material events from first oncology referral through the consent conversation and treatment decision.
When she says 'the notes,' she means the core legal bundle: EPR entries, consent forms, MDT record, clinic letters, and policy documents already retained in the claim file request.
An 'initial expert view' means a short desktop screening opinion from one external oncologist based on the papers only, not a full merits report.
The 'MDT discussion' relevant to the case is the formal tumour-board meeting closest to the disputed treatment decision, because that is the one likely to matter evidentially.
Contacting clinicians this week means asking them to preserve recollection and availability for later witness statements, not requesting substantive written narratives yet.

members.name: Daniel Morris
members.expertise: Healthcare governance, incident response, disclosure coordination, and liaison with clinical divisions and risk teams
members.background: Daniel came from an in-house NHS governance pathway and regularly manages complaints, coroner prep, and pre-action information gathering across oncology and surgery services.
members.private_state: Daniel wants to use the case plan to surface any systemic practice issues around guideline use and shared decision-making before they become reputationally damaging, and he is concerned that late internal fact-gathering will leave clinicians feeling blindsided.
hidden_assumptions: A 'chronology' at planning stage means an operational chronology compiled from all available records, including complaints correspondence, incident reviews, scheduling data, and patient-information leaflets, so everyone has the full story.

When he hears 'the notes,' he assumes this includes the complete trust record set around the episode: nursing notes, booking logs, patient portal messages, complaint file materials, and any related governance documents.
An 'initial expert view' means a preliminary internal clinical review from the trust’s oncology clinical director or governance lead to orient the legal team before spending money externally.
The 'MDT discussion' includes both the formal tumour-board entry and the earlier corridor/planning exchanges and pre-MDT case-review emails that shaped the recommendation.
Contacting clinicians early means asking them now for concise factual accounts while memories are fresh, because that is standard pre-action preparation inside the trust.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prepare 'the chronology and issues list.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this is a narrowly framed, privileged legal chronology limited to events directly bearing on breach, causation, and consent.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this is a broad operational chronology including complaints, governance reviews, scheduling events, patient-information materials, and surrounding administrative context.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal-healthcare work, 'chronology' is a routine term that both use confidently, and each assumes the other naturally understands the standard scope from their own practice setting; the companion phrase 'issues list' reinforces a false sense that the deliverable is already well defined.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will pull 'the notes' before drafting begins.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the core evidential clinical and policy documents needed for external legal assessment: oncology records, consent forms, MDT minute, clinic letters, and applicable guideline/policy extracts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the entire trust-side documentary universe around the episode, including nursing records, appointment logs, portal messages, complaint correspondence, and governance materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both work in disputes where saying 'the notes' normally suffices, and neither expects the other to need a list of inclusions because each assumes their version is the obvious baseline for competent preparation.

misalignment_points.topic: Who provides the initial expert view
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to get an 'initial expert view' before finalising the response position.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to instruct an external independent oncologist for a short privileged desktop screening opinion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to obtain a preliminary internal view from the trust’s oncology clinical director or governance reviewer first, and treat that as the initial expert input.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase focuses attention on the shared goal—getting medically informed orientation—while concealing the method; both routes are common enough in practice that neither sounds remarkable when referred to generically.

misalignment_points.topic: Which MDT discussion is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need to understand 'the MDT discussion' before speaking with counsel.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the formal multidisciplinary team meeting on 14 March recorded in the tumour-board minute.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader decision sequence, especially the pre-MDT email exchange and informal case huddle on 12 March that shaped the recommendation before the formal meeting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In oncology cases, people routinely collapse multiple decision-making moments into the shorthand 'the MDT discussion'; because both believe they are pointing to the same recommendation process, the referential mismatch feels too minor to flag.

turns.inner_thought: We only have three days before the drafting session, so I need a litigation-ready starter pack rather than a sprawling internal exercise. For me the chronology and issues list should be a tightly framed, privileged legal chronology from referral into oncology through the consent conversation and treatment decision, with a short issues grid on breach, consent, causation, and guideline use. I do not want broad governance traffic muddying the first pass before I've seen the oncology file.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Daniel. Just to frame it, the threatened claim is really pitching two points together: that the treatment pathway was too guideline-led, and that the patient says the decision-making and consent process weren't properly individualised. With the drafting session coming up, I'd like us to have the chronology and issues list ready beforehand so counsel can get straight to the key points.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. If they're invoking that article about evidence-based medicine being in crisis, this could turn into a wider criticism of service culture if we're not careful. When she says the notes, I assume we need the full trust-side record set around the episode, not just the headline oncology papers: nursing entries, booking history, portal messages, complaint correspondence, incident material, leaflet versions, all of it. Better to surface context early than discover later that clinicians feel we've ignored obvious background.
turns.utterance: Yes, I agree. It's a sensitive angle because they're not just criticising a single decision, they're effectively saying the service defaulted to protocol over shared decision-making. I'll start pulling the notes today, along with the surrounding materials, so we're not trying to reconstruct this at the last minute.

turns.inner_thought: Good. The first package needs to stay narrow enough to send to chambers without unnecessary internal noise. I want the treatment decision, the consent pathway, and the formal tumour-board meeting closest to the decision—the 14 March MDT minute—because that is what will matter evidentially. If counsel can see those core liability documents quickly, we can decide what else is worth chasing.
turns.utterance: That sounds sensible. For the first package, I'd keep the emphasis on the treatment decision, the consent pathway, and the MDT discussion, so counsel can see the main liability points quickly without us overcomplicating the opening pass.

turns.inner_thought: I'll make sure the MDT discussion is captured properly, but for me that absolutely includes the lead-in, not just the formal board note. In oncology these recommendations are often shaped before the meeting by emails and short huddles, and if there was later governance or complaint commentary touching the same point, I want that in the chronology as well. The whole point is to understand how the recommendation evolved, not just what landed in the final minute.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll make sure we capture the MDT discussion in full, including what was circulating beforehand and any follow-up context that may help explain how the recommendation was reached.

turns.inner_thought: Once I have the core papers, I want a short privileged desktop screening opinion from an external oncologist. Not a full report, just enough to orient us on breach and consent before we harden the response. I do not want to lock ourselves into any trust-generated merits position before seeing the full oncology record.
turns.utterance: The other thing I'd like us to do is get an initial expert view next week, before we finalise the response position. That should help us judge how firm we want to be on breach and consent.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. I can get a preliminary internal clinical steer quickly once the notes are together; the oncology leadership team already knows the service background and can tell us whether there are any obvious practice issues around guideline use or shared decision-making. That will be much faster and more useful at this stage than spending money externally before we've mapped the operational picture.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. Once the notes are in hand, I can line that up quickly because the oncology leadership team already knows the service background, so we should be able to get an initial expert view without much delay.

turns.inner_thought: I should tighten the scope now so the chronology doesn't balloon. I mean referral, oncology review, consent appointment, recommendation, immediate aftermath—enough to analyse legal exposure. The issues list should stay disciplined and not wander into every surrounding complaint or systems point before we've established the core merits.
turns.utterance: In terms of structure, I'd like the chronology to start at referral and run through the consent appointment, the treatment recommendation, and the immediate aftermath. And I'd keep the issues list quite tight at this stage.

turns.inner_thought: That works, and within that frame I still want the operational story visible. If there were scheduling delays, leaflet version changes, or a complaint trajectory that shows how the patient's concerns developed, those belong in the chronology in my mind. Otherwise legal will miss the context that could become reputationally awkward later.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll fold in the complaint timeline, the patient-information leaflet versioning, and any scheduling points as well, so the chronology reflects the whole picture rather than just the headline clinical events.

turns.inner_thought: I need the formal MDT material before I speak to chambers, and I do want clinicians contacted this week—but only to preserve recollection and availability for later witness work, not to invite substantive accounts that create unnecessary documents before we've scoped the case. I'll keep this high level because Daniel should know the usual drill.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll speak to chambers once I have the MDT material. In the meantime, can you make sure the clinicians are contacted this week so we're not leaving that too late?

turns.inner_thought: Absolutely. Early factual accounts are standard and clinicians hate being approached months later as if this has appeared from nowhere. I'll get the consultant and CNS team to provide concise factual narratives now while memories are still fresh, which should also help us identify any governance themes before they harden into a defence problem.
turns.utterance: Yes, I'll reach out to the consultant and the CNS team for short factual accounts while recollections are fresh. That should give us a cleaner base for the rest of the preparation.

turns.inner_thought: Let's pin responsibilities down. Daniel can assemble the core legal bundle and the lawyer-facing chronology by Monday; I do not need an unwieldy record dump, but I assume he'll know what matters. I'll arrange the external desktop expert screening and draft preliminary issues headings in a privileged format so we can move quickly with chambers.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Let's work to Monday for the first package: you'll assemble the notes and the chronology by then, and I'll arrange the initial expert view and put together the preliminary issues headings so we have something coherent before the drafting session.

turns.inner_thought: Monday is workable. By then I should have the fuller trust record, the broader chronology, and the relevant decision-making context around the MDT discussion. Once that material is compiled, we ought to be in a good place both legally and from a governance perspective, even if Amira is mainly thinking about counsel's immediate needs.
turns.utterance: Monday works. Once the MDT discussion and the notes are compiled, we should have what we need to move efficiently and avoid scrambling in the drafting session.
